title: B is for BEST GLIDE SPEED: The single most critical number when things go wrong | MSFS A-Z
description:
Picture this: You're cruising at 5,000 feet, enjoying the view, when suddenly—absolute silence. Your engine just quit. Your heart drops and panic sets in. You have only a few minutes before you meet the ground, and every single second counts. In this scenario, there is exactly one airspeed that stands between you and a catastrophic crash landing. If you fly too fast, you bleed altitude too quickly. If you fly too slow, you risk a deadly aerodynamic stall.

Welcome back to Microsoft Flight Simulator A to Z! In this episode, we are tackling the fundamental savior of forced descents: the letter B for Best Glide Speed. We break down the core aerodynamic theory of how your wings trade potential energy (altitude) for forward airspeed, why this lines up with your aircraft's maximum lift-to-drag ratio ($L/D_{max}$), and where to find this critical number across light general aviation planes and high-fidelity third-party airliners. Finally, we take a Cessna 172 up to 4,000 feet, starve the engine of fuel, and walk through manual trim management, scanning for forced landing sites, and surviving a chaotic glide over tight terrain, trees, and hidden power lines.

In this video, you’ll discover:

- The Theory of Vbg: Why pitch control acts as your ultimate altitude economy mode when the cockpit goes completely quiet.
- Drag Mechanics Simplified: Visualizing the intersection where parasitic drag and induced drag drop to their lowest combined value.
- The Pilot's Checklist: How to pull reference speeds from real-world POH manuals, MSFS documentation, and cockpit Electronic Flight Bags (EFB).
- Emergency Flight Demo: Step-by-step physical recovery, manual yoke adjustments, and using the trim wheel to lock in 68 knots hands-free

🕒 Chapters
00:00 - Intro
00:46 - The Theory (Vbg & Drag Mechanics)
01:51 - Where to find your Vbg
02:44 - Demo: Step-by-Step recovery

Understanding how to preserve your altitude as energy separates casual flight simmers from real-world virtual pilots. Before your next cross-country flight, open up your aircraft's manual, memorize your Vbg speed, and ensure you're ready when the engine goes silent.
